sec.title: Background
sec.p: Opioid-induced cough (OIC) is a common side effect during anesthetic induction. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of ketamine/esketamine in preventing OIC during anesthetic induction.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We systematically searched Medline, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar from inception through December 2024 for randomized controlled trials that examined the efficacy of ketamine/esketamine in preventing OIC (Registration: INPLASY2024120102). Studies were included if they: (1) evaluated surgical patients receiving short-acting opioids (e.g., fentanyl) during anesthetic induction; (2) compared ketamine or esketamine against placebo/no treatment; and (3) reported OIC incidence. Studies were assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2.0 tool. Random-effects meta-analysis was performed using risk ratios (RR) for dichotomous outcomes and mean differences (MD) for continuous outcomes, with 95% confidence intervals (CI). The primary outcome was the overall incidence of OIC within 3 min after opioids administration.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Twelve trials involving ketamine (nine trials) and esketamine (three trials) were analyzed. Notably, both agents significantly reduced the overall incidence of OIC compared to placebo (RR: 0.30; 95% CI: 0.22–0.41; p < 0.00001, I2 = 61%, moderate certainty). All studies demonstrated low risk of bias across all domains for primary outcome. These agents also demonstrated efficacy against mild cough (RR: 0.41, 95% CI: 0.28–0.59, high certainty) and moderate-to-severe cough (RR: 0.26, 95% CI: 0.18–0.38, moderate certainty). The intervention delayed cough onset by 2.77 s (95% CI: 1.25–4.29, moderate certainty) and showed mild improvement in oxygen saturation (MD: 0.55%, 95% CI: 0.15–0.95, high certainty) without significant effects on heart rate or blood pressure. Subgroup analyses confirmed consistent benefits across adult and pediatric populations, as well as between ketamine and esketamine.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Our findings suggest that ketamine and esketamine are effective in reducing OIC during anesthetic induction. However, given the short delay in cough onset and mild improvements in oxygen saturation, the clinical significance of these findings may be limited in routine practice. Their use may be most beneficial in selected patients at risk of OIC-related complications. Further research is warranted to assess their value in high-risk populations and their role in combination prevention strategies.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Opioid-induced cough (OIC) is a common and potentially concerning side effect that occurs during the induction of general anesthesia, particularly with rapid administration of short-acting opioids [1–4]. While often self-limiting, this reflexive cough response can result in significant physiological effects, including marked increases in intracranial, intraocular, and intra-abdominal pressures[5], which may pose risks in patients with pre-existing head trauma, glaucoma, or abdominal hernias. In some cases, OIC can manifest explosively, causing significant discomfort to patients [6]. Furthermore, several case reports have highlighted the occurrence of airway obstruction or pneumonia following OIC [7, 8], indicating that the occurrence of OIC is not without carrying subsequent complications. OIC can affect 21.8–75% of patients receiving fentanyl and its analogs [4, 9, 10], affecting both adult and pediatric populations [11, 12]. This high prevalence underscores the importance of recognizing and addressing OIC in diverse patient groups, as its occurrence may complicate the perioperative course and require tailored management strategies. The mechanism underlying OIC involves complex interactions between opioid receptors and various neural pathways, including the stimulation of rapidly adapting receptors in the upper airway and activation of vagal nerve afferents [3, 13]. Considering that fentanyl and its derivatives (e.g., sufentanil, remifentanil, and alfentanil) are widely used in the induction of anesthesia, prevention of OIC may be clinically important.

N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor antagonists, such as ketamine and esketamine, are well-established in anesthetic practice and possess unique properties that may effectively suppress cough. Evidence suggests that NMDA receptor antagonists play a critical role in regulating the cough reflex while also exerting a direct relaxant effect on airway smooth muscles [14, 15]. This dual action sheds light on the potential mechanisms and therapeutic targets for managing OIC. A previous network meta-analysis compared five different pharmacological interventions (lidocaine, ketamine, dezocine, butorphanol, and dexmedetomidine) and found that dezocine showed the highest efficacy in preventing OIC, followed by butorphanol and ketamine [16]. However, this analysis [16] did not comprehensively examine the role of esketamine, nor did it address vital clinical considerations, such as hemodynamic stability and recovery profiles associated with the administration of ketamine and esketamine. Evaluating these issues is crucial for understanding the overall risk–benefit profile and optimizing the use of these agents in clinical settings, particularly in diverse patient populations with varying risk profiles.

To compensate for this knowledge gap, we conducted this systematic review and meta-analysis with the following hypotheses: (1) ketamine and esketamine would effectively prevent OIC during anesthetic induction; (2) both agents would demonstrate comparable efficacy and safety profiles; and (3) their benefits would be consistent across different patient populations. Our research questions examined: (1) ketamine and esketamine efficacy in preventing OIC; (2) their impact on hemodynamic stability and recovery; and (3) the consistency of their effects across different patient groups. Our study aimed to extend previous research [16] by providing the first comprehensive analysis of esketamine's role in OIC prevention, assessing previously unexamined clinical parameters such as hemodynamic stability, recovery profiles, oxygen saturation changes, and analyzing the consistency of effects across diverse populations and regions. Additionally, the previous analysis [16] was limited to five studies on ketamine, our broader review includes more trials, providing more robust evidence for clinical decision-making. Through this analysis, our findings will offer clinicians strong evidence to inform their perioperative care practices.

sec.title: Method
sec.p: The protocol for this systematic review and meta-analysis was registered on the INPLASY platform, a dedicated registry for systematic reviews. The registration can be accessed via the INPLASY website at https://inplasy.com/inplasy-2024-12-0102/, with the unique registration number INPLASY2024120102. The report of the current meta-analysis was prepared in accordance with the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines.

sec.title: Search strategy
sec.p: We conducted a systematic literature search using Medline, Google Scholar, Embase, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) from inception through December 2024. The search strategy combined Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms and free-text keywords and incorporated three main concept groups: intervention terms, including Ketamine, Esketamine, N-methylaspartate receptor antagonists, NMDA, and S-ketamine; short-acting opioids, encompassing Opioid, Fentanyl, Remifentanil, Sufentanil, and Alfentanil; and outcome terms, focusing on Cough, Respiratory Reflexes, and Airway Reflexes. These terms were combined using appropriate Boolean operators and adapted for each database. The detailed search strategies for Medline were available in Supplemental Table 1. Similar search strategies were adopted for the other databases. We also manually screened the reference lists of the included studies and relevant reviews to identify additional eligible trials. We contacted the corresponding authors when additional data or clarification was needed. No language restrictions were applied.

sec.title: Study selection and inclusion criteria
sec.p: We included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated the efficacy and safety of ketamine and esketamine in preventing OIC. Studies were considered eligible if they met the following criteria: (1) included surgical patients of any age receiving short-acting opioids (i.e., fentanyl, remifentanil, sufentanil, or alfentanil) for anesthetic induction; (2) compared ketamine or esketamine with either a placebo or no treatment; and (3) reported the incidence of OIC as either a primary or secondary outcome. The titles and abstracts of the retrieved articles were screened by two independent reviewers based on predefined eligibility criteria. The full texts of potentially eligible articles were obtained and evaluated independently by the same reviewers. Discrepancies were resolved through consultation with a third reviewer.

Observational studies, case reports, reviews, animal studies, and trials that did not report relevant outcomes were excluded. Additionally, studies that combined ketamine or esketamine with other agents (e.g., dexmedetomidine or lidocaine) to prevent OIC were also excluded. For studies with multiple arms comparing ketamine/esketamine alone or in combination with other agents with placebo, only the intervention arm involving ketamine/esketamine alone was included.

sec.title: Quality assessment
sec.p: Risk of bias was assessed at the outcome level using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2.0 tool in accordance with current guidance [17], with two reviewers independently conducting the evaluations. This tool evaluates five domains: the randomization process, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, outcome measurement, and selective reporting. For the randomization process, we evaluated whether the studies employed appropriate randomization methods and maintained adequate allocation concealment (e.g., sealed opaque envelopes). For deviations from intended interventions, we assessed the blinding of participants, healthcare providers, and outcome assessors, examining whether studies used identically appearing interventions and whether protocol violations occurred. Regarding missing outcome data, we evaluated completion rates, reasons for withdrawals, and handling of missing data in the analyses. For outcome measurement, we assessed whether assessors were blinded and measurement methods were standardized, with particular attention to subjective outcomes such as cough severity grading. For selective reporting, we compared outcomes listed in methods/protocols against those in the results sections. Each domain was categorized as having a"low risk,""some concerns,"or"high risk"of bias. Any discrepancies between the reviewers were resolved through discussion or by involving a third reviewer.

sec.title: Outcomes
sec.p: The primary outcome was the overall incidence of OIC within 3 min after opioid administration, regardless of severity. Secondary outcomes included (1) severity of cough (mild and moderate-to-severe cough), which was defined based on individual studies; (2) hemodynamic changes (i.e., heart rate and blood pressure) within 3 min after opioid administration, with blood pressure measured by mean arterial pressure (MAP) or systolic blood pressure when MAP was unavailable; (3) onset time of cough, defined as the time from opioid administration to the first cough episode; and (4) oxygen saturation changes. For outcomes measured at multiple time points, we collected data closest to opioid administration (preferably 1 min) to capture the immediate effects during the period when OIC is most likely to occur.

sec.title: Data collection
sec.p: Two independent reviewers extracted the data using a standardized form. Extracted information included study characteristics (first author, publication year, country), participant demographics, intervention details (ketamine/esketamine dosage, timing), opioid characteristics (type, dose), and predefined outcomes. For studies reporting incomplete data, we contacted the corresponding authors. Disagreements were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer.

sec.title: Certainty of evidence
sec.p: We assessed the certainty of evidence for all outcomes using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) framework. This approach considers the following domains: risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias. Each outcome was graded as"high,""moderate,""low,"or"very low"certainty. The initial certainty of evidence for each outcome from RCTs was rated as high but could be downgraded based on the identified concerns in the domains. The final certainty ratings for each outcome are summarized in a GRADE evidence profile table.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: All statistical analyses were conducted using a random-effects model to account for potential variability among the included studies. The effect sizes for dichotomous outcomes were calculated as risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), whereas continuous outcomes were expressed as mean differences (MD) with 95% CIs. Sensitivity analyses were conducted to evaluate the robustness of the findings by systematically excluding each study individually. Heterogeneity among studies was quantified using the I2 statistic. I2 values of 25%, 50%, and 75% were interpreted as representing low, moderate, and high heterogeneity, respectively. When significant heterogeneity was detected, potential sources were explored using subgroup analysis. Subgroup selection was based on the clinical and methodological factors influencing treatment effectiveness. Age groups (adult vs. pediatric) were compared because of physiological differences in airway sensitivity and varying responses to opioids and NMDA antagonists. The intervention type (ketamine vs. esketamine) was examined because esketamine, as ketamine's S(+) enantiomer, has different potency. The geographic region was analyzed to account for genetic variations affecting opioid receptor function and ethnic differences in drug efficacy. Publication bias was assessed visually using funnel plots for outcomes with at least 10 included studies. All analyses were performed using Cochrane Review Manager (RevMan 5.3; Copenhagen: The Nordic Cochrane Center, The Cochrane Collaboration, 2014), and two-tailed p-values of p < 0.05 were considered statistically significant.

sec.title: Study selection
sec.p:
A total of 310 records were identified from the database searches, including Medline (n = 41), Embase (n = 67), Cochrane Library (n = 97), and Google Scholar (n = 105) (Fig. 1). After removing 63 duplicates, 247 records were screened for titles and abstracts, resulting in the exclusion of 224 irrelevant studies. The full texts of 23 reports were assessed for eligibility, and no reports were excluded due to retrieval issues. However, 11 studies were excluded for the following reasons: 4 were review articles, 3 were conference abstracts, and 4 lacked an intervention group. Twelve studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in the final review [18–29].Fig. 1
Study selection process for the current meta-analysis

sec.title: Characteristics of studies
sec.p:
The studies were conducted across six countries: Iran (five studies), China (four studies), Turkey (one study), Korea (one study), and Taiwan (one study) (Table 1). All studies were published between 2007 and 2024, with the majority conducted in adult populations, except for two studies by Shafa et al., which focused on pediatric patients [26, 27]. The mean age of the adult participants ranged from 34 to 69 years, with male representation varying between 25 and 70%. The sample sizes ranged from 60 to 360 participants. All participants were classified as American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) physical status I-II, except for one study [23] that included patients with ASA II-III. Regarding interventions, both ketamine and esketamine were studied, with dosages ranging from 0.1 to 0.5 mg/kg for ketamine [19–22, 25–29] and 0.05 to 0.2 mg/kg for esketamine [18, 23, 24]. Most studies administered ketamine/esketamine 1 min before opioid administration, with one study using a 5-min interval [21]. All studies used saline as the control. The opioids investigated included fentanyl (doses ranging from 1.5 to 4 μg/kg), sufentanil (0.4–0.5 μg/kg), and remifentanil (1 μg/kg or 5 ng/ml). The reported incidence of OIC varies considerably across studies, ranging from 20 to 100%. Follow-up times were predominantly short, ranging from 1 to 3 min post-opioid administration.Table 1

sec.title: Risk of bias
sec.p:
For the primary outcome, all studies were rated as low risk across all five domains (Fig. 2), including the randomization process, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, outcome measurement, and selection of reported results. Consequently, the overall risk of bias for each study was rated low. Outcome-specific RoB 2 assessments for secondary outcomes are presented in Supplemental Table 1, with all outcomes judged to have an overall low risk of bias.Fig. 2
Risk of bias assessment for the 12 included studies. The green circular icon indicates a low risk of bias

sec.title: Outcomes
sec.p:
Our meta-analysis of 1,968 patients demonstrated that ketamine and esketamine significantly reduced the overall incidence of OIC compared with placebo (Fig. 3). The intervention group experienced significantly fewer cough events (127/1019 patients, 12.4%) than the placebo group (355/949 patients, 37.4%), representing a relative risk reduction of 70% (RR: 0.30; 95% CI: 0.22–0.41, p < 0.00001, I2 = 61%). All studies consistently favored the intervention over placebo, with RRs ranging from 0.02 to 0.56. Further analysis according to cough severity revealed significant benefits across all categories. For mild cough, ketamine/esketamine demonstrated substantial efficacy, with 7.6% (74/979) of patients in the treatment group compared to 16.7% (152/909) in the placebo group, resulting in a relative risk reduction of 59% (RR: 0.41, 95% CI: 0.28–0.59, p < 0.00001, I2 = 30%) (Fig. 4). The intervention was even more effective in preventing moderate-to-severe cough, demonstrating a relative risk reduction of 74% (RR: 0.26, 95% CI: 0.18–0.38, p < 0.00001, I2 = 32%) (Fig. 5).Fig. 3

In a meta-analysis of 950 patients from five studies, ketamine/esketamine significantly delayed the onset of OIC by 2.77 s (95% CI: 1.25–4.29, p = 0.0003, I2 = 71%) (Fig. 6). The high heterogeneity for this outcome (I2 = 74%) likely stems from differences in measurement techniques and the timing of assessments across studies. While statistically significant, the absolute duration (2.23 s) is likely too short to meaningfully contribute to smoother anesthetic induction in clinical practice.Fig. 6

Ketamine/esketamine delayed cough onset by 2.77 s (95% CI: 1.25–4.29; p = 0.0003), suggesting statistical significance but limited clinical impact. CI: Confidence Interval; Ke: ketamine; Esk: esketamine

Regarding hemodynamic parameters, the intervention demonstrated a similar safety profile. Analysis of 1,539 patients showed no significant impact on heart rate (mean difference: −0.16 bpm, 95% CI: −3.42 to 3.10, p = 0.92, I2 = 85%) (Fig. 7). The high heterogeneity in heart rate measurements (I2 = 85%) can be explained by variations in the baseline cardiovascular status of participants, differing anesthetic protocols, and the timing of measurements across studies. Similarly, blood pressure remained stable between both groups (mean difference: −0.54 mmHg, 95% CI: −2.47 to 1.38, p = 0.58, I2 = 55%)(Fig. 8). Interestingly, oxygen saturation showed a slight improvement in the ketamine/esketamine group compared to that in the placebo group (mean difference: 0.55%, 95% CI: 0.15–0.95, p = 0.007, I2 = 63%) (Fig. 9). Even minor improvements in oxygenation during the vulnerable period of anesthesia induction can provide an additional safety margin, particularly in elderly patients or those with pulmonary comorbidities. Recovery parameters were also assessed, showing no significant impact of ketamine/esketamine on extubation/awareness time (mean difference: 1.73 min, 95% CI: −1.59 to 5.05, p = 0.31, I2 = 83%) (Fig. 10). The high heterogeneity in recovery times (I2 = 83%) likely reflects differences in anesthetic protocols, varying definitions of recovery endpoints, and the subjective nature of assessing awareness and readiness for extubation. These findings suggest that ketamine/esketamine pretreatment can be administered without affecting vital signs or recovery time. Fig. 7

sec.title: Subgroup analyses
sec.p:
For age-based analysis, both adult and pediatric populations showed significant reductions in OIC, with RRs of 0.29 (95% CI: 0.21–0.41, I2 = 52%) and 0.35 (95% CI: 0.15–0.79, I2 = 77%), respectively (Table 2). The analysis revealed no significant difference in the treatment effect between the adult and child subgroups (P = 0.70). Regarding the intervention type, both ketamine and esketamine demonstrated comparable efficacy. Ketamine showed a RR of 0.31 (95% CI: 0.22–0.43, I2 = 60%) across 12 datasets involving 1,452 participants (Table 2). Esketamine demonstrated similar effectiveness with an RR of 0.25 (95% CI: 0.08–0.77, I2 = 76%) in 3 datasets including 516 participants. The difference between these interventions was not statistically significant (P = 0.75). Geographic subgroup analysis revealed consistent benefits across different regions (Middle East: RR 0.23, 95% CI: 0.12–0.43, I2 = 78%); East Asian: RR 0.36, 95% CI: 0.27–0.50, I2 = 40%). The test for subgroup differences also suggested no significant variation in the treatment effect between geographic regions (P = 0.19) (Table 2). Table 2

sec.title: Sensitivity analysis and publication bias
sec.p:
Sensitivity analysis was performed across various outcomes to assess the robustness of the results. The analyses indicated consistent findings for the majority of outcomes, whereas the sensitivity analysis for cough onset time revealed inconsistent results (Table 3). Regarding publication bias, evidence of potential publication bias was identified for the overall incidence of cough (Supplemental Fig. 1) and moderate-to-severe cough (Supplemental Fig. 2), while no publication bias was observed for mild cough (Supplemental Fig. 3) or heart rate (Supplemental Fig. 4) after opioid administration. For other outcomes, such as cough onset time, publication bias assessments were not performed because of the limited number of studies (< 10). Table 3

sec.title: Certainty of evidence
sec.p: The GRADE assessment revealed a high certainty of evidence for mild cough, blood pressure changes, and oxygen saturation (Table 3). Moderate certainty was found for the overall incidence of cough, incidence of moderate-to-severe cough, cough onset time, and change in heart rate due to inconsistency, publication bias, or imprecision concerns. Low certainty was assigned to extubation time/awareness owing to inconsistency and imprecision concerns.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined 12 RCTs and demonstrated that ketamine and esketamine were highly effective in reducing the overall incidence of OIC during anesthetic induction. Both agents showed consistent effectiveness across mild and moderate-to-severe cough categories, while delaying cough onset by approximately 3 s. Compared to placebo, both agents demonstrated similar hemodynamic profiles while showing mild improvements in patients'oxygen saturation levels after opioid administration. Recovery and extubation times remained unaffected, supporting their practical application in clinical settings. Subgroup analysis showed that the benefits are consistent across different agents (ketamine vs. esketamine) and populations (adult vs. pediatric patients), and remain effective across various geographic regions. The GRADE assessment indicated a high certainty of evidence for mild cough prevention, blood pressure stability, and oxygen saturation improvements, while other outcomes showed moderate to low certainty.

Our findings demonstrate that ketamine and esketamine provide robust protection against OIC during anesthesia induction. The substantial reduction in cough incidence suggests that these agents effectively modulate the complex neural pathways involved in the cough reflex. This protective effect aligns with our current understanding of NMDA receptor antagonism and its role in cough suppression [14, 15]. The consistency of this preventive effect across different study populations and settings strengthens the evidence for clinical implementation. Notably, the protective effect remained significant despite variations in opioid types and dosing regimens, suggesting broad applicability in anesthetic practice. These findings expand upon a previous meta-analysis [16], which was limited to five studies that focused solely on ketamine without assessing the efficacy of esketamine. This broader review provides a more comprehensive understanding of the roles of both ketamine and esketamine, highlighting their potential as effective interventions for preventing OIC and addressing the gaps in previous research.

The protective effects of ketamine and esketamine against OIC add to their established benefits during anesthetic induction. These NMDA receptor antagonists are well known for their ability to maintain hemodynamic stability during anesthesia induction, particularly in preventing propofol-induced hypotension through their sympathomimetic properties and preservation of baroreceptor reflexes [30, 31]. Ketamine and esketamine are also recognized for their analgesic properties and ability to reduce perioperative opioid consumption [32–34]. By incorporating these agents into the induction protocol, primarily for cough prevention, clinicians may simultaneously benefit from their opioid-sparing effects and potential reduction in immediate postoperative pain. Recent evidence has shown that the use of ketamine and esketamine is associated with an improved subjective quality of recovery following surgery [35] as well as a reduction in postoperative depression [36]. This multimodal benefit aligns with the current enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) protocols. Furthermore, both agents have demonstrated neuroprotective properties and may help reduce the incidence of postoperative delirium and cognitive dysfunction [37]. Their anti-inflammatory effects might also contribute to improved postoperative outcomes [38]. The timing of administration for cough prevention—typically just before opioid administration—coincides well with capitalizing on these additional benefits during the crucial period of anesthetic induction.

Several methods have been reported to effectively reduce the risk of OIC during anesthetic induction. These include Huffing’s maneuver, preemptive administration of opioids, and the use of pharmacological agents such as lidocaine, dexmedetomidine, and dezocine [1, 39–42]. A previous network meta-analysis indicated that ketamine exhibits moderate efficacy in preventing OIC, ranking third among the five agents studied (lidocaine, ketamine, dexmedetomidine, dezocine, and butorphanol), followed by dezocine and butorphanol [16]. While not achieving the highest efficacy, ketamine offers several distinct advantages in clinical practice that merit consideration when selecting an antitussive agent. Unlike dezocine, which shows superior efficacy but has limited availability in many countries, ketamine is widely available and is commonly stocked in most anesthesia departments. This accessibility, combined with its well-established safety profile and familiarity among anesthesiologists, makes ketamine a pragmatic choice, despite its relatively low efficacy ranking. When comparing ketamine to dexmedetomidine and lidocaine, ketamine demonstrates superior efficacy while offering a similar ease of administration. All three agents can be readily incorporated into existing anesthetic induction protocols. However, the higher cost and longer onset time of dexmedetomidine may limit its practical utility. While lidocaine has fewer psychomimetic effects, the potential benefits of ketamine and esketamine in preventing postoperative delirium and cognitive dysfunction may offer additional value in certain patient populations [37, 43], making the choice between agents dependent on specific patient needs and clinical contexts.

The combination of ketamine or esketamine with non-pharmacological interventions may provide enhanced protection against OIC. The huffing maneuver, which involves forced exhalation through an open glottis, has shown efficacy in cough prevention by modifying airway sensitivity [39]. When combined with pharmacological agents such as lidocaine, this maneuver demonstrates synergistic effects in reducing cough incidence [4]. Similar synergistic benefits may be achieved by combining ketamine or esketamine with non-pharmacological techniques. Future research should investigate the potential synergy between ketamine/esketamine and various non-pharmacological methods such as the huffing maneuver, slower opioid injection rates, and priming techniques. Such combinations could potentially allow for reduced ketamine/esketamine dosing while maintaining protective effects against OIC, thereby optimizing the risk–benefit profile of perioperative cough prevention strategies.

Ketamine and esketamine may prevent OIC through multiple mechanisms, in addition to NMDA antagonism. They interact with μ- and κ-opioid receptors [44], attenuating tracheal mucosa sensitivity while simultaneously inhibiting voltage-gated sodium channels to suppress cough-triggering C-fiber transmission [44, 45]. These agents can also directly relax airway smooth muscle by blocking calcium influx and modulating intracellular calcium release, significantly reducing airway sensitivity to irritants during the post-opioid administration period [46, 47]. Combinations with dexmedetomidine may enhance antitussive effects of ketamine/esketamine through complementary mechanisms: ketamine primarily acts via NMDA antagonism and direct airway effects, whereas dexmedetomidine modulates sympathetic activity and reduces airway sensitivity through vagolytic actions. Similarly, combining lidocaine with ketamine simultaneously blocks sodium channels (lidocaine) while inhibiting central sensitization and smooth muscle contraction (ketamine).

The findings of this meta-analysis have significant implications for anesthetic practice, healthcare policy, and future research in the field of perioperative medicine. Based on this meta-analysis, we recommend incorporating ketamine (0.1–0.5 mg/kg) or esketamine (0.05–0.2 mg/kg) administered 1 min before opioid delivery into anesthetic induction protocols for ASA I-II patients. The strong protective effect against opioid-induced cough (70% risk reduction) coupled with stable hemodynamics and unaffected recovery times justifies their routine use. However, institutional guidelines should acknowledge current limitations, including the predominance of data from East Asian and Iranian populations, limited follow-up periods, and lack of studies in high-risk patients. We suggest a tiered approach in which ketamine/esketamine are the first-line agents for standard-risk patients while maintaining flexibility for individualized protocols in high-risk cases. Future research priorities should address these gaps through multicenter trials with diverse populations, extended follow-up periods, and inclusion of ASA III-IV patients, while also focusing on optimizing dosing protocols, investigating potential long-term outcomes, and conducting cost-effectiveness analyses. Particular attention should be directed toward expanding the evidence base for esketamine, which shows promising results but currently has limited data compared to ketamine.

Our meta-analysis has several important limitations that should be considered when interpreting the results. First, the age distribution in our population was heavily skewed toward middle-aged adults, with only two pediatric studies and no focused geriatric populations, creating significant gaps in our understanding of age-specific responses. Second, the geographic concentration of studies primarily in East Asia (China, Taiwan, and Korea) and Iran may affect the broader applicability of findings across different healthcare systems and ethnic groups. Third, most studies had remarkably short follow-up periods (1–3 min), leaving uncertainty about potential delayed effects and long-term safety (e.g., hallucination and dizziness). Fourth, the majority of participants were classified as ASA I-II, with only one study including ASA III patients, limiting the generalizability to higher-risk populations. Fifth, substantial heterogeneity exists in intervention protocols, with ketamine dosing ranging from 0.1 to 0.5 mg/kg and esketamine from 0.05 to 0.2 mg/kg, while opioid types and doses also varied considerably. Sixth, potential publication bias, evidenced by asymmetrical funnel plots for the overall incidence of cough and moderate-to-severe cough, may have led to overestimation of the treatment effects. Finally, the relatively small number of studies examining esketamine (only three trials) warrants caution in drawing definitive conclusions about the comparative efficacy of esketamine. Future research should address these limitations through multicenter trials with diverse populations, standardized protocols, and longer follow-up periods to strengthen the evidence for clinical practice recommendations.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Based on this meta-analysis, ketamine and esketamine demonstrated compelling efficacy in preventing OIC during anesthetic induction, providing a robust evidence base for their clinical application. The significant reduction in cough incidence, coupled with the effectiveness across severity levels and a favorable safety profile, supports their integration into standard anesthetic protocols. However, these findings primarily reflect immediate outcomes within 1–3 min after administration, and long-term effects remain undetermined. The consistency of benefits across diverse patient populations (e.g., adults and children) and geographic regions, along with the comparable efficacy between ketamine and esketamine, offers clinicians flexibility in agent selection. The absence of significant adverse effects on hemodynamic parameters and recovery times further strengthens their clinical utility. Future research should explore the optimal dosing regimens for different patient populations, potential synergistic effects when combined with non-pharmacological interventions such as the huffing maneuver, long-term safety and efficacy beyond the immediate induction period, and comparative effectiveness in high-risk patients with significant comorbidities.
